speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE PLEBISCITE
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-ADJOURNMENT OVER VOTING DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware the voting with respect to the removal of restrictions on the government aris-

The Plebiscite
ing out of past commitments as to the method of raising men for service overseas takes place on Monday of next week.
I believe hon. members generally feel it would be of assistance to others if they were privileged to be in their constituencies on Monday, at the time the vote is being taken. I am sure it would greatly facilitate the work of organization if they could be present in their constituencies not only on the day of actual polling but as well a day or two in advance. As the house does not sit on Saturday or Sunday, and as the sitting on Friday is only for a half day, in the opinion of the government it would be of real assistance if hon. members could be in their constituencies one or two days immediately preceding the taking of the vote, as well as on the day on which the actual vote is taken.
We realize of course that in provinces which are some distance from the capital it might not be possible for hon. members to return to their constituencies. However if the house were to adjourn on Thursday evening, after concluding Thursday's proceedings, only half a day in the present week would be lost, and the only day in the next week would be Monday, the day of polling.
In those circumstances during my absence the acting leader of the government communicated with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and the leaders of the two other parliamentary groups with respect to ascertaining their views as to adjourning for the time indicated, and I am informed there appears to be general agreement that an arrangement of that kind would be satisfactory.
If I were to make a motion at this time unanimous consent of the house would be required. If unanimous consent were not given I would give notice of the motion in to-day's Votes and Proceedings, and if discussion were desired it could be discussed later. But I believe it would perhaps be to the advantage of all if a decision could be arrived at immediately.
The leader of the opposition has, I understand, been kind enough to intimate that he is prepared to second the motion I may make in this connection, and I wish to thank him for so doing. In the circumstances, with the consent of the house I move, seconded by the leader of the opposition:
That when the house adjourns on Thursday, the 23rd instant, it stand adjourned until Tuesday, the 28th instant.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE PLEBISCITE
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-ADJOURNMENT OVER VOTING DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not understood that I was to second this motion, but I shall say at once that when the matter was brought to my attention late last week I agreed with the substance of the proposal
now before the house. I am so strongly impressed by the urgent necessity of an affirmative vote by the people of Canada on Monday next to release the government from its commitments that I think it of very great importance that all hon. members who think as I do should be in their constituencies for the vote, and should exercise all the influence they can through personal contact with the voters in those districts.
I regret that the idea did not germinate sooner, because some hon. members from western Canada would like to participate as well. Obviously that is now impossible. However, for the reasons I have given, those outlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and others which must be obvious to every hon. member, I suggest that unanimous consent be given.

maintopic: THE PLEBISCITE
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-ADJOURNMENT OVER VOTING DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too gave approval
to the suggestion when it was telephoned to me by the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty). But in doing so I had considerable misgiving. I felt that some hon. members adjacent to this city might be able to assist in bringing out an effective vote, and that we should place nothing in their way if they were so disposed. But we had had a very long recess, during which we had all been in touch with our constituents, and it seemed to me that we should have done everything then that we felt it necessary to do to this end.
I also regret that the intimation was not given until Friday of last week, which made it impossible for those coming from western Canada to remain in their constituencies. I feel that paihament at this session has been lagging in the work that has to be done. So far no war expenditures committee has been appointed. The committee on radio has not met, and we have a large amount of committee work ahead of us. I believe the general feeling throughout the country is that we are not making the progress, with regard to measures relating to the war, that we ought to be making. It is my view that this feeling of dissatisfaction with this parliament may be reflected in the vote on Monday next. I urge the government to see to it that we do not further delay our proceedings, that the committees which ought to be sitting be appointed forthwith, and that we get down to the business of the session more expeditiously than we have done during the past two months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The tug Bally was chartered by the naval service on the 8th December, 1939. As the vessel required extensive repairs to continue on the duties upon which she was employed and as the department purchased a more suitable vessel, the owner was advised to take delivery of the vessel at Halifax on the 9th September, 1941. The owner did not take delivery and was again notified on the 14th November, 1941, that from the 9th September, 1941, the department would assume no responsibility with regard to the vessel, its stores and appurtenances.
By letter dated 30th October, 1941, the owner advised the department that he preferred to loan the vessel to the department until the spring of 1942, if no other arrangement could be made, as he considered it unsafe to bring her to Charlottetown during the winter.
Charter fees have not been paid beyond the 9th September, 1941, nor has the department assumed any responsibility with regard to the vessel, its stores and appurtenances since that date.
Due to the expansion of the naval service, it is possible that the vessel would be suitable for other purposes without the necessity of extensive repairs required for her original duty. The possibility of utilizing the vessel for other purposes is under consideration, but a decision with regard to her re-charter has not yet been reached.

[Mr. Howe.l

maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	Published maps of the Geological Survey, Canada, show the areas in New Brunswick where the presence of coal is considered possible. Investigations of the survey from 1866 to present indicate the strong probability that workable coal in New Brunswick is restricted to a single seam (18 to 26 inches thick), the one already being mined. Results of a special investigation of the Grand Lake coalfield accompanied by geological maps of the field were published in 1926 and formed the basis of further detailed investigations by the provincial geologist of New Brunswick from 1935 to present. Because the workable coal is confined to a single seam within a nearly flat-lj'ing thin surface rock formation, there are no outstanding problems of geology remaining to be solved that would further exploitation; nor has the government of New Brunswick made any requests for specific investigations upon which action has not been taken.
Systematic drilling is the main requirement as a preliminary to further production. By its use present producing companies have extended the workable areas and increased coal production in 1940 by 82 per cent over the average production for the past ten years.
The fuel laboratories of the Department of Mines and Resources have made many tests on New Brunswick coal. The results of this work demonstrated that New Brunswick coal could be materially improved by washing and sizing and that a substantial reduction in ash took place. It was also shown that not only could a good coke be prepared by utilizing a low temperature carbonization process but also that an excellent coke could be produced when the washed coal was processed in the Curran Knowles by-product coke ovens.

which also was passed as an order of this house on May 22, 1940, and to my surprise I find that the return to this order has never been brought down.

This session I saw a lady member, whose constituency I have forgotten, bluffed out of her right just as cold-bloodedly as I have ever seen anything done. The privilege of moving resolutions has been taken away from us, and we dare not protest at all, or somebody points the finger of scorn

The bill to be based upon the resolution is really a continuance or extension of the Youth Training Act which was sponsored by the late Minister of Labour, the Hon. Norman Rogers, and which set in motion the youth training plan of that day. From its inception until 1941, three hundred thousand persons have received training under that legislation. The act expired on March 31 of this year. The intent of the new bill is not only to maintain that system of training in which the provinces and the municipalities cooperate to the fullest extent, but also to extend its scope so as to make provision for a number of additional training schemes. The war emergency training programme must be carried on. It is fair to say that the groundwork laid by the youth training plan made possible the quick and extended war emergency training programme that exists at the present time. It might fairly be said of the late Minister of Labour that he planned better than he knew, with the result that at the outbreak of the war we had perfect cooperation between the federal government and the provincial governments and municipalities in order to set in motion an enormously extended programme that made possible the training of men and women for war industries as they exist to-day.

Moveover, it has rendered very considerable assistance to the Royal Canadian Air Force, the navy, and the armed forces.
The purpose of the bill is so that the cooperation with the provinces and municipalities shall be carried on and largely extended as the need arises, with the inevitable expansion of war industry. It will provide training facilities for such unemployed workers as may require training under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act. That act provides for the training of unemployed workers and it is the intention that the machinery set up
thereunder, and the training facilities, shall be made use of. That responsibility will be assumed for the unemployment insurance commission. Provision will also be made for vocational training for persons discharged from the armed forces in the present war, and in the post-war period the foundation will be laid and provision will be made for the training of returned men as they come back from overseas-that is, those who require training. In the last war, I may say frankly, a magnificent job was done without any previous experience in the training of men returning from overseas. I have a vivid recollection of having a number of trainees working under me at that time, and at the conclusion of training they all found employment with the firm with which I was working.
The framework of the bill allows of projects being undertaken either directly by the dominion or to be carried on by agreement with the provinces. At the present time, in some instances, the cost of the training programme is shared fifty-fifty by the federal government and the provinces, and in other instances the cost of equipment is shared on an equal basis. In still other instances the cost is paid wholly by the dominion. In connection with preliminary training for the Royal Canadian Air Force, the navy and the army, the whole cost is borne by the government.
No specific sum will be mentioned in the bill because of the uncertainties of the situation and the conditions that confront us. Estimates will have to be introduced every year for the purpose of carrying out training under the bill. As I have pointed out, inasmuch as training for the army, the air force and the navy is primarily the responsibility of the dominion, that is assumed in toto by the dominion. I think a great deal of credit is due to the provinces and the municipalities for the assistance rendered the dominion not only prior to the outbreak of war but since then. They have placed at the disposal of the government technical schools which in some cases have been operating on a twenty-four hour basis, and they have also provided teachers and teaching staffs. I need hardly tell hon. members that the dominion had not the facilities for creating immediately an organization of this kind. We have had that decentralization which in the final analysis is sometimes the best form of government when it is closest to the people.

That being so, the minister may declare that any industry is not an essential industry, and that therefore he can drive every young man in this country, by the back-door route, into enlistment for active service overseas. That is the absolute truth, and it is a shameful policy. If "cowardly" is not a parliamentary term, I shall use the expression "shameful policy"- and I believe I am stating the truth.
What has happened in connection with these young trainees? A young lad is about to attain the age of call. He is called by the Department of National War Services presided over by the minister from Selkirk. Before his call goes out, his name is given to the recruiting officer in the district in which he lives. Mark you, this is before he is called. This is another indirect approach on the part of the government to get recruits by the voluntary system-and we are told how wonderfully it is working! He gets a letter from the chief recruiting officer in- the area telling him that he is going to be called, and by a more or less polite paragraph in the letter he is advised that he had better sign up for the active army. He may do so or he may not, but I want to tell the minister and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) that so far as that recruiting officer is concerned, that young man is a marked man the minute he gets into the training centre.
I have evidence of the case of a young man in a county in Ontario who is in- the nonactive army. He has been approached repeatedly by the non-commissioned officers and asked to enlist for active service. He has applied for a furlough to go home to see his family, but this has been refused although his furlough is long past due. He has been

Vocational Training

told that if he will sign on the dotted line, for active service, he can go home on a double furlough. What kind of recruiting system is that? That is a travesty on British justice.

No, I do not; I am advocating something quite different. I am advocating a manly, straightforward system. I believe the Minister of Labour, if he were free, would advocate this also. In fact, within the week he probably has advocated it. How can he retain his selfrespect and remain in a ministry that will adopt such methods? I do not just understand why methods such as those to which this administration has resorted should be adopted in order to get recruits for the active army. While the objective is excellent, I want to say that the methods resorted to in order to obtain men for the active army for service anywhere are everything that they should not be. The methods vary. One method will be adopted in one recruiting area, and another will be adopted in another area. Much will depend upon the resourcefulness of the recruiting officer or the degree to which he is hard-hearted or hard-boiled. Some of these fellows are pretty hard-boiled and they will resort to anything. I have heard of cases where physical pressure has been applied, where a man was blackened because he would not sign up. I have heard of one recruiting area where they got 100 per cent of the trainees to enlist for the active army by methods which I believe could not bear the light of day.
Let us get away from this sort of thing. I think this has been admitted on the floor of this house. Let us not be extreme in our language. But I want to say to the minister that there are many things that I believe he would not approve. I think we agree as to the objective, that is, to get men into the active army to defend this nation, and I shall talk about that to-night, but we ought to revise our methods.

Last week I sat on an examination board examining voluntary recruits for the Lanark and Renfrew Scottish regiment. The hon gentleman has just raised another point which has not been touched upon in the debate this afternoon. During the padt year the war emergency training programme 'has accorded the veterans of the present war and of the great war a preference in accepting candidates for training. Subsistence allowances have been paid to those selected for such training, and employment has been found for trainees in war industry. I am replying directly to the point raised by my hon. friend.
The war emergency training programme has developed from the youth training facilities, and is carrying on in conjunction with the provincial governments and in close association with educational bodies throughout the dominion. These arrangements in respect of vocational training have laid a useful foundation for cooperation between the youth training organization of the Department of Labour and the Department of Pensions and National Health in respect of vocational training of discharged men which will be very helpful, we hope, in the difficult period that lies ahead.
This committee will recall that last year the rehabilitation committee, in a comprehensive report to the parliamentary committee during the past session, filed a recommendation in respect of vocational training which goes far beyond the narrower view of vocational training established at the end of the last war. At that time vocational training facilities were restricted to those with pensionable disabilities who were unable, on account of disability, to resume their previous employment, and to minors. It is recognized, however, that many men now serving had little opportunity prior to enlistment to acquire a skill, and unfortunately many of them have not had the discipline or training of a job. The subcommittee on vocational training therefore recommended:
That training should be given those who on the recommendation of competent vocational guidance officers are considered by age, aptitude and inclination as likely to benefit from such training.
This recommendation, together with the recommendation of the subcommittee on interrupted education suggesting that provision be made for resumption of interrupted education, and reports of other subcommittees,

were given coherence in what is known as the post-discharge reestablishment order, passed on October 1, 1941.
The provision made for subsistence allowances in respect of vocational training is wide, and such allowances will be payable by the Department of Pensions and National Health. That department is now proceeding to establish a vocational training division with a competent and experienced director to carry on the work.

I am astonished to hear my hon. friend take any objection to that method. It is the only way whereby you can allocate the man-power of this country. The man who is physically fit and of military age can either be doing a military job or be in civilian employment. The man who is not physically fit and is not of military age cannot do a military job, but he may do a civilian job; and the method to which my hon. friend refers is intended to provide that the older and less fit man is put into that civilian job, and the other man is left free to do the job which his neighbour cannot do. I do not think my hon. friend) should take objection to that. I think it is part of any selective service system. To see to it that young men who are physically fit and of military age are not employed in non-essential industries is, I believe, a perfectly proper system. Furthermore, I think the matter might be put in another way. One of the essential purposes of any sound national selective service system is that as far as possible every person in the country, whether man or woman, shall work in that field of war activity where he or she can best promote the total war effort. Another purpose of any sound selective service system is to avoid wastage of man-power in comparatively nonessential industries, in the case of men who are physically fit for active service and of military age. The purpose of passing this order restricting the entry of certain persons into a number of occupations was, in the first place, to prevent a wastage of manpower. These occupations have a very large turnover; and when any person who is at present engaged in one of these occupations ceases to be employed therein, it is intended that that person's place shall be filled either by a woman or by a man above military age or unfit for military service. That in a broad way is national selective service. The various regulations which were discussed by the Prime Minister on March 24, indicate the attitude
Vocational Training

of the government in this matter. There are two possible approaches to a national selective service system. One is to try to assess the individual qualifications of every man and woman in the country, and ticket them, and move them round from place to place. That task in itself would take an army of people who would be much better engaged ' in doing something else to promote the war effort. The other approach is a much more practical and realistic one. The government has announced its war programme; it has announced its programme for the armed forces and for munitions production, both programmes in terms of man-power requirements; the purpose of our national selective service system is to assist in meeting those requirements in a practical and realistic way, meeting situations as they arise by means of regulations, seeking also to anticipate by regulations situations which are likely to arise; in other words, meeting specific conditions by specific measures. I believe that is a much more practical and more realistic approach to the whole system of national selective service than the first approach would be. The order to which reference has been made is part of that system. It restricts the entry into a certain number of occupations of men who are of military age and physically fit for the armed forces. All the occupations are listed in the schedule. All are comparatively non-essential, or if they are essential they can be filled either by women or by older men or men unfit for military service. This is the kind of national selective service which every one has been urging, and this is a realistic and practical way of putting it into effect. The persons who are prevented from entering these occupations are not barred from entering essential war activities.

Mr. COLDW'ELL: Yes, you did. It is exactly what you said.

speechtext: If I said it I regret it. It is not the interpretation I meant to put on my own words.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: I think the policy is clear. If I were an able-bodied young man I would be in the fighting forces. They are the aristocrats of their day. If it were not for these young men, there would not be any House of Commons. I think that is perfectly obvious. I took that position in the last war and I take it in this war. I do not know why I should waste any time over able-bodied men of military age, single -men.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
The minister is saying in one breath that the policy of the government is that these men shall be able to go into war industry, and in the next breath he says that so far as he is concerned

and he is the man who has the administering of the order in council-these men have no right to go into war industry.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: That is what it amounts to.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: I suggest to the minister and to other members of the ministry that the house and the country are entitled to know what "the government's policy is on this question. Let us know, and then let the employers comply with that policj\ Do not have this business of the government having one policy and winking ait the employer following another. We cannot expect to have a wholehearted war effort under such conditions. The country is entitled to better leadership than that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
My good friend the
Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) put the case very nicely, as he always does, but it is no less economic conscription. Then -my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), who is not so particular about putting things nicely, asked why he should lose any sleep over an ablebodied man who is not in one of the services. Buit the government that he represents, the government whose policies he has adopted, took the position that they would not by law compel any man to go into the armed services.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: By the direct route.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: But now they are putting him into the armed services through -his stomach.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL

This is not a condition that has arisen since the orders in council were -passed; it has -been going on for many months. This is what it amounts to. The poor man who has no one to keep him will starve or go into the armed forces. He will starve unless he already has a job. Economic conscription applies to him, but it does not apply to the young, physically fit -man whose father can keep him, or whose father is in a position to keep him.

speechtext: I assure you it would not.

speechtext:
It possibly would not, but the fact is there. I am not saying how many it applies to. I am telling my hon. friend that it is the government's policy at the present time to put the poor man into the armed forces through starvation, while the rich man's son is not affected. speechtext:
I should like a little
further information. I listened with interest to the remarks of the Minister of Pensions
Vocational Training

and National Health, who seemed to have right at his finger-tips just what he wishes to achieve along these lines. But I am trying to find out whether this bill covers what the minister has in mind.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: I agree with the objective the minister has in mind, but the resolution refers to a measure to provide for the promotion of vocational training projects, and it does not specify returned men only. When I first read it over I was of opinion that it was very much along the lines laid down by the Minister of Labour when he first outlined the proposal, at which time he followed more or less the proposals of his predecessor, the late Mr. Rogers. Am I to undersand now that the bill does not cover any but returned soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: The Department of Labour advises that preference for discharged men was embodied in the war emergency training programme regulations which became effective on January 1,1941. Since that preference was instituted, until February 25, 1942, discharged men have been admitted to training forces to the number of 3,002. The Department of Labour further advises that the number admitted to training in the month of February of this year was 282 men, discharged during the present war. The Department of Pensions and National Health paid the training benefits to discharged men under the post-discharge order, to which I referred, passed on October 1, 1941, to 285 veterans during March, 1942, involving an expenditure of $11,802.06. That is under the terms of the post-discharge order, one of which benefits is this vocational training, and these figures indicate how that is progressing even though at the present time it is only in its very early stages.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
This afternoon a good deal was said about young men being trained

under this programme, and it was stated that in order to enjoy these benefits they would be forced to enlist in the army. That has not been denied. The matter was dealt with by the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Vancouver East; as a matter of fact hon. members from Vancouver seem to be in the thick of it to-night, between the Minister of Pensions and National Health and the two hon. members I have mentioned, who seem to understand the bill pretty well. Those two hon. members were under the impression that under the bill w'hich will be founded on this resolution, in order to obtain these benefits young men would be forced to join the active forces, whether or not they wanted to do so. I should like some further information along that line. I have been wondering just how the bill will fit in with the present scheme sponsored by the manufacturers of aeroplanes. In the vicinity of Toronto, for instance, the aeroplane companies secure a great deal of their help, many of their men and, I presume, their women also, since now they have thousands of women working in their plants, through the central technical school, where they send them to take courses lasting several weeks or several months before they enter the plants. Will this vocational training scheme fit in with that scheme which is now in operation?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes. That is already
part of the scheme.

speechtext: And it is a very worthy part of it. That matter was taken up with my predecessor and myself. The view expressed by the department was that we could not subsidize permanent buildings, because the building suggested would take perhaps eighteen months to construct, and there is ample space available of a temporary nature that could be put to use almost immediately. The provincial government was sounded out in this connection also, and that was why the representations of the city of Toronto were not looked upon in a kindly way by the federal government.

Vocational Training

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: The representations were not looked upon in a kindly way by this government but they were supported by the provincial government, who said they would cooperate. That, however, is something quite apart from this bill, and perhaps I should not have brought up the subject. Let me conclude with this. Was the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Vancouver South correct, that in order to obtain benefits under the bill to be founded on this resolution young men will be compelled to enlist in the active army?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: Could we clear up that point a little? We are told that those who attend these schools are not forced to enlist in the active army. They do enlist to this extent, that after they complete their training and pass the medical examination they are automatically in the army.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: That is so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: I do not think that is altogether correct. We have what are called pre-enlistment classes, and also classes for enlisted men. For instance there are preenlistment classes at Galt and many other centres in connection with the air force. Some of those men go into the air force and some go into industry.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
We have a motion to appoint a committee to consider a proposed bill to assist in the carrying on and coordination of vocational training. Parliament has not been in session for the last three weeks. Primary things should come first. The war is primary; the appointment of this committee is secondary. We do not know where we are to-day, so far as the war is concerned. Since parliament adjourned for the recess, we have suffered heavy losses on the seven seas, and the very fate of civilization has been at stake. How will the appointment of a committee advance this vocational problem? I have been in the house for many years, and I have failed to see how any committee has made progress on any public question, so far as section 91 of the British North America Act is concerned.
The minister is new to the department, and no doubt he is anxious to do certain things. But I can tell the committee that the country wants parliament, now that it is back here in Ottawa, to act and to get on with this war, and not just to talk about it. In my opinion the appointment of committees to consider these domestic questions should wait, and it is the function of this government to handle this question and not just deal in windowdressing.
As a former member of a school board I have had some experience in this matter. It will be recalled that the Laurier government appointed a commission to investigate technical education, and to give special attention to technical and vocational training as applied to secondary schools and trade and industry. A report made to the government of that day pointed out that it was the function of the federal parliament to take that action, because it controlled trade and commerce. We control finance, banks and banking and matters of that kind, and for that reason vocational and technical training is a function for which this parliament is solely responsible.
There can be no doubt that, after the war, vocational training will be of great importance, and especially since it is applied to soldiers on reestablishment in civil life. 1 believe, however, that sooner or later we shall have to consider education of this kind. The report dealing with vocational training, as a part of technical education, showed the necessity of parliament taking on this task here.
After the war the wreckage will be so great that there will be nothing to salvage. No one will want to be in industry, or connected with trade. With all the bureaucratic boards established by orders in council almost every day we meet, how can any businessman deal with vocational training in his business or aid it after the war in his industry. I fail to see how it can it be done.
What has been done in England? They have not appointed committees, as we have done. Over there the government has accepted the onus of responsibility. While I have sympathy with the present proposal in principle, may I point out that Toronto was a poineer in matters affecting vocational and technical training. Technical and vocational schools were established in that city. Every day between 10,000 and 12,000 day and night students attend those schools, and in the evenings between 7 o'clock and 10 o'clock students meet to study. All this is done at the city's expense. The government does not do a thing for those schools or give them any direct aid. Those technical schools in Toronto are doing a fine work in matters of vocational
Vocational Training

training and war work, and yet the government will not grant one cent, although war industries seek their graduates eagerly. Federal power should assist this work by grants and other aids.
I hold in my hand some pictures showing the wrnrk in Toronto's technical central school in connection with acetylene welding. I believe the first technical school in Canada was established many years ago in Toronto. Students from those schools are going to the industries engaged in manhfacturing munitions, and in canying out other war work. The schools have applied to the minister's department to obtain a grant for a new wing to the central technical school, because some of the students are now working in an old garage on Bathurst street on war work. The main school building in which all forms of technical work are now carried on cost about SI,500,000 with plant and additions. They are doing war work, and because of that the board of education came to Ottawa asking that it be given a small grant for a new war wing for these enlisted war workers and students. But the government turned a deaf ear to that application.
As I see it, after the war the wreckage in industry will be so great that there will be nothing left to salvage, and no one will want to be in trade and commerce. What has been done in England? A bill known as the trade and commerce bill has been passed by both houses of parliament. That bill has reestablished in Great Britain certain pre-war trade practices. Because of that action industry and trade and commerce know where they stand. On the other hand, in Canada we have the cart before the horse. Win the war first, and then take up all these domestic questions.
On an earlier occasion, when this matter was under discussion I asked the minister what the policy of the government was. I asked questions regarding all these bureaucratic boards which have been established throughout the country, placing impossible barriers and artificial burdens on business. A certain businessman told me he has three or four clerks who do nothing but get information and file these returns.
What is the function of government? We have been refused information by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) with respect to one board dealing with a feature of war work- the commodity price corporation. No doubt if this measure passes, some corporation or board will deal with vocational training, despite the fact that we have been refused information as to how this price corporation money has been spent, and the price paid. About a week ago the chairman of one of

these boards gave an interview to a reporter on the Toronto Globe and Mail in which he gave detailed information the Minister of Finance had declined to give to parliament two weeks before.
I have no objection in principle to a committee on vocational training. Although nothing has been said about it yet here in the house, I have no doubt that, after the war, commercial aviation will accord a great opportunity for vocational training to a great degree and provide work, because I believe it will constitute one of our most important transportation facilities. At the present time, however, I believe this motion is purely academic, and nothing can be accomplished by it at this time. It is based entirely on winning the war. While I am in favour of the principle of the resolution, I believe the onus is on the government to carry on this soldier education programme in conjunction with the provinces and the various boards of education across Canada and secure real vocational training at cost and avoid duplication and waste by coordination now absent.
It is all moonshine to talk about planning after the war when at this very moment Britain is fighting for her very life and existence. We do not know where we shall be. We were beaten in January and February, on the Pacific and on the seven seas. It is all very well to say that we are enjoying a party truce, but at present it is very much onesided. It may be that in some respects we are enjoying a party truce. However. I just came from one of the Toronto constituencies where certain gentlemen in one party have appeared and preached about this planning, and matters of that kind, in a purely socialistic way and do not observe the party truce to win the war. Let us deal with war problems first. It is all very well to talk about vocational training. I appreciate what it has done for the returned soldier, and I realize that after the last war it was most commendable, although very much delayed at the start. But at that time it was a non-partisan effort. In my opinion any action along this line in the future should be taken in conjunction with the provinces, and especially with the boards of education, to avoid overlapping and duplication, and federal power must aid post-war education.
The university of Toronto, through all her graduates, has been a pioneer in this matter. In my opinion the appointment of this committee will not do any good. The executive can do this work better. We must get on with the war, which is primary, and whioh is not secondary to these domestic questions.

Vocational Training
While I am in sympathy with everything done for the soldiers along this line, I believe there has been too much playing with this question, and unless we give it more careful consideration we shall accomplish very little. This committee will be like the war expenditures committee, which found out practically nothing. The report of that committee has not even been discussed here, and the report of this committee will be too late for any action till after the war.
I have had some experience with these matters, and in my view we ought first to lay down future principles with respect to industry, trade and commerce, and particularly agriculture in Canada. We must decide whether industry is going, after the war, as it is now, to be placed under all thes-e burdens and barriers in restraint of trade with which industry is now faced. Some of those regulations may be all right, but large portions of industry are affected by them all, and we know that many of the regulations will not help by one iota to win the war. We must first break the shackles of bureaucracy by which trade and commerce are bound now in Canada, hand and foot, before we shall be in a position to support vocational training in industry. We must break these shackles with which trade is now bound, hand and foot, by some such act as in England to restore pre-war trade practices.
There are legions of men sitting in offices who pass these regulations of price boards with respect to trade and industry, so that no man can conduct his business. The small, independent businessman is being driven out of business and cannot function or shift his industry to aid vocational training. All parties in the house have supported vocational training. At the close of the last war we were not properly prepared. In this matter of education we might very well give grants to the provinces and local school boards. Certainly before very long we shall have to go into education, on a very elaborate scale. Further, this bill must take care of these apprentices who have gone to the war, and place them back in their industries to continue on.
Labour and industry could be united; they are united. The contribution of labour has been most magnificent in this war as has that of industry and employers, and I do not think we would have been able to do what we have done had it not been for labour. Labour, agriculture and industry are united in a magnificent effort.
We should develop the resources of this country to their limit. In water-power, only 7,000,000 horse-power have been developed when we have 42,000,000 horee-power available. Next year Great Britain will face the
greatest coal shortage in her history, and we may be suffering here while our natural resources in coal and substitutes are allowed to lie dormant. I believe we should first lay down the principle of where trade and commerce are to be to-day and to-morrow, and where they will be after the war, if industry will be enabled to support the policy of the government which they want to do when the war ends, and after the war all bureaucratic boards should go.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: Despite anything that was said this afternoon, I am supporting this resolution, and I believe it will receive general support from the whole committee. We find ourselves at the present time with a pressing work to do, that is, war production, and not enough trained workers to do it. I imagine the first purpose of this vocational training will be to fit men and women for war work. That is most important. It is proper that we should consider questions of this kind now. Not only shall we need it to-day; we shall need it equally when the war is over. As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) said quite rightly this afternoon, it is in line with the work initiated by the late Norman Rogers when he was Minister of Labour. I do not know, and possibly I shall not know until the bill is brought down, what age ranges will be covered by this measure. Will it be restricted to young people?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: No limit.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: I am glad of that. In my opinion our aim should be to fit every man and woman in Canada for some job, and provide a job for every man and woman in Canada. We should not be satisfied with anything less than that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: A chicken in every pot.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes; two automobiles in every garage. That was promised at one time, but not necessarily here. There is only one way of getting a chicken in every pot and a car in every garage, that is by getting our men and women producing those things. They do not fall out of the skies. I was always a little suspicious of the story about the manna. The minister has said that there will be no age limit. Our aim should be to train every man and woman in Canada for work. When we fit people for work, not only are we making them capable of producing useful things, we are recreating them. To the extent that this measure will perform that function, I am certainly in support of it.
Vocational Training

There is nothing that destroys everything that is worth-while in a man as quickly as unemployment and the feeling that he has no useful place in the community.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: To what extent are men and women over forty-five years of age being given vocational training at this time? There is a great need for the training of older men and women. That would be in line with the government's policy of restricting the entry into industry of men between the ages of seventeen and forty-five years. It does seem most important that the older men and women should be given this training. To what extent has that been done?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I would point out to my hon. friend that I have been close to this war emergency training programme since its inception. I was one of those who helped to draft it. The emphasis has always been placed upon the training of older men. Those of us who thought we saw the development of this war were convinced that sooner or later young men would be drawn into the army, navy and air force and that there would be a shortage. At the moment I can tell my hon. friend that of those between the ages of thirty and thirty-nine years, there are 3,505 being trained; between the ages of forty and forty-nine, 1,915, and fifty years and over, 737. I met many manufacturers, as well as the manufacturers' association, and the emphasis was always placed on this point. We all appreciated that there was a spill-over from the depression to the war and that many young men were out of employment, but we felt that sooner or later the time would come when these younger men would have to go into the fighting forces, or at least would go into the fighting forces, and that then a demand would be created for the older men.
I am convinced that we must consider the woman problem as soon as we possibly can. Personally I do not think we have scratched the surface of the man-power available in this country. A year from now the women of this country will be doing things they never dreamed of doing in the past.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: What steps are being taken to get these people into war work or into the training classes? Are you advertising that these courses are available?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: For older men and women?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: It is well known through the employment services and other agencies established by the government.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: This afternoon I asked the minister what I thought was a most pertinent question with regard to the council, but I do not think he got to the point of answering it. Is this to be a voluntary committee or are the members to be paid? What is to be the character of the committee? What will be its functions?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to the advisory committee?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext: Yes. I understand that there is a voluntary advisory committee in Toronto which is doing good work without any cost to the government. maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR

speechtext:
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to make provision for the settlement on the land of veterans of the present war, to prescribe the terms of such settlement and to grant a measure of financial assistance to such settlers, and further for the appointment of a director, of officers and other employees in connection therewith.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Vien in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a statement to the committee in regard to the principles of the bill to be introduced provided this resolution is approved by the committee. The resolution precedes a bill to be known as the Veterans' Land Act. It is one of the measures resulting from the work on the committee on demobilization and rehabilitation and its several advisory committees and subcommittees. The bill to be introduced has three main purposes: first, to assist discharged members of the armed forces 
to establish themselves successfully in the farming industry in Canada; secondly, to ensure that the agricultural industry bears its share of the rehabilitation problem along with other phases of our industrial life; thirdly, to give ex-members of the forces returning to agricultural pursuits benefits comparable with those available for men entering other occupations. .
In this last connection it should, perhaps, now be pointed out in the first place that discharged men entering insurable employment are credited with the time spent on military service since July 1, 1941, and the government of Canada-the people of Canada-pay the premiums; second, that employers are compelled to reinstate exmembers of the forces in their former positions; third, that discharged men who have no trade may be given vocational training and their families maintained by the state while they are undergoing such training; fourth, that young men whose education was interrupted may be supported while completing their educational course and their tuition fees may be paid by the state; fifth, that former civil servants have their positions and their security of superannuation preserved for them; and lastly, that discharged men who are temporarily incapacitated and also those who are capable of and awaiting work may be paid benefits or grants of S9 a week for single men and $13 a week for married men for a period up to fifty-two weeks.
It will be seen, therefore, that some similar measure of assistance for those who undertake farming is fully justified on the grounds of equity.
This bill differs in many vital respects from the Soldier Settlement Act adopted during the last war. These differences are based upon a study of the history of the former soldier settlement plan, which was admittedly by no means the success hoped for both by the country and by the ex-servicemen who went on the land under its provisions.
I come now to the terms of the Soldier Settlement Act.
Under the Soldier Settlement Act the country advanced $109,034,331 for the establishment of 24,793 soldier settlers and 224 Indian soldier settlers-just over 25,000 in all. The great bulk of the settlement, as hon. members are aware, took place in 1919 and 1920. Of the original number of settlers there remained on the land as at March 31, 1941, approximately one-third, namely 8,118

Veterans' Land Act
settlers. On March 31, 1941, the situation with regard to these approximately 25,000 settlers was as follows:
Remaining on their land .. ..	8,118
Paid off their loans	 2,750
Sold out their equities	 884
The remainder, 13,041; had abandoned the scheme either voluntarily or by notice.
On March 31, 1941, total recoveries from the original advances were S65.640,518. This includes payments made by civilian purchasers to whom foreclosed properties have been sold. The recoverable value of the outstanding loans is estimated at not more than $30,000,000, which would make a gross recovery of $95,640,518, as against an original capital investment of $109,034,331. These recoveries represent an estimated capital loss of $13,393,813, all interest payments actually made having been included in the $65,000,000 of recoveries already mentioned. The administrative cost from 1918 to March 31, 1941, stood at $25,910,495.
The primary reasons for this state of affairs are, I think, to be found in the following facts. When the operations were begun there was available no staff fully trained in settlement operations. Second, in the period when the bulk of the settlement took place, prices paid for land, chattels and building materials were influenced by war-time inflation. The depression beginning in 1931 brought about a serious deflation in these values. Third, all advances were repayable with interest at 5 per cent; consequently the settler was placed under a burden of debt, including land, live stock and equipment, which often represented 125 to 150 per cent the value of the land. In an effort to remedy these defects the following measures were taken:	in the first place, the
consolidation of loans; second, cancellation of interest charges for a certain period; third, revaluation of land; fourth, 30 per cent horizontal reduction in the debt in 1930; fifth, a bonus system, subject to the payment of taxes by the settler, whereby a credit of $2 was given for every $1 paid; and lastly, adjustment of contracts under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. These deductions totalled $47,518,215 as of March 31, 1941.
Other factors contributing to the high degree of failures may be mentioned as follows. Seventy per cent of the establishments took place under very difficult conditions in the prairie provinces. The difficulties encountered by all farmers in their communities arising from drought and market fluctuations were shared by the soldier settlers. All establishments were predicated upon the settler deriving his living and his main income from the land. Many could have been better assisted by considering the farm as merely a home, the main income of the family being derived from employment. In the new bill to be presented, the government has profited, I think, by the experience gained under the Soldier Settlement Act, and the major difficulties have been avoided.
I now come to the chief differences between the old act and the one to be introduced.
There are three vital differences between the present bill and the Soldier Settlement Act of the last war, as well as a number of minor differences. The three chief differences may be described as follows:
First, whereas the Soldier Settlement Act contemplated that settlers should give their full time to their farming ventures, the present bill is broad enough to assist men in taking up small holdings where the veteran will make his home and derive a substantial portion of his income from employment apart from his cultivation of the land.
Second, the benefits of this measure are confined to persons who were domiciled in Canada upon enlistment and who served in Canadian or imperial forces. The former act covered members of the forces of the allies. It is felt that since this act provides a subsidy by the dominion government, the benefits should not be extended to other than prewar residents of Canada unless there is a reciprocal arrangement.
The third and greatest difference is that no soldier settler under this bill will be encouraged or permitted to assume an uneconomic and unbearable burden of debt. This necessarily involves a direct grant by the state, which in some instances may represent almost 50 per cent of the total cost of the enterprise.
In broad outline, the proposed scheme contemplates that an applicant for assistance must satisfy the director in charge of administration not only that he wishes to engage in farming, but that he has the qualifications for that occupation. In this connection there is provision for training, at public expense if necessary. In order to ensure that the veteran shall have a personal stake in the success of his enterprise, it is an absolute condition of the bill that the veteran himself shall make a cash payment at the outset equal to 10 per cent of the cost of the land, improvements and building materials upon which a loan is to be issued. Under the old act there was authority to waive any csah contribution by the settler, and experience has clearly shown that this was a mistake.
Veterans' Land Act

A vital principle of this bill is recognition at the outset that the average veteran under typical conditions cannot be expected to provide a living for himself and his dependents and maintain the farm plant in working order and pay annual taxes, and in addition thereto meet the payments required, if his indebtedness is for practically the full cost of the land, improvements, live stock and farm equipment. This principle was not recognized in the original provisions of the Soldier Settlement Act, and failures under that act were largely due to the hopelessness of the debt structure, notwithstanding a series of remedial amendments.
The bill embodies the principle that the debt assumed by the veteran shall not exceed two-thirds of the cost of the land and buildings, or, if the maximum costs permitted by the bill are reached, the debt will not exceed 50 per cent of the cost of the whole enterprise, including stock and equipment. The state contribution, subject to specific performance by the settler, is a grant equal to one-third of the cost of the land and buildings, and a further grant of the cash cost of the stock and equipment furnished to the veteran. On a maximum basis the annual payment required from the settler is $144. This sum, in addition to his annual taxes, is. believed to be such as the average veteran can successfully pay while providing a reasonable standard of living for himself and his family.
If justification be needed for the policy of making a grant, it is to be found in the following considerations.
In a country like Canada it is futile to say that land should not play an important part in the rehabilitation of ex-service men. Second, industries other than agriculture will be expected to absorb the majority of exservice men, and other industries cannot be expected to meet the total problem. Third, the experience gained in the operation of the Soldier Settlement Act and similar projects in other countries shows that without such assistance the average veteran stands but a limited chance of establishing home ownership within his working lifetime. Fourth, following every former war in which Canada was engaged, there were valuable ungranted crown lands available for distribution among veterans. That situation no longer exists to-day so far as the federal government is concerned.
Under the relief settlement agreement with (the provinces of Quebec, Manitoba and Alberta, more than 10,000 families have been assisted to settle on the land by means of an unrecoverable grant of $1,000 per family. In Manitoba the amount was $1,250 per family, and in Quebec the grant was increased to $2,000 per family. It is estimated that the

cost of the grant made by the state in the average case under the proposed bill will be $1,360. Assistance is being made available to the ex-service man who wishes to become a lawyer, a doctor or a skilled workman, under provisions previously passed. It is felt that similar assistance should be given those who wish to become farmers.
Before proceeding to explain the chief provisions of the bill I think it is desirable to refer briefly to another important consideration. Under the Soldier Settlement Act of 1919, establishments were in the main predicated upon the soldier settler deriving his main income from the land upon which he was established. Similar provisions are contained in this bill, but it is sufficiently flexible to provide for a wide range of establishments involving the use of land. It is contemplated that establishments may be on a full-time farming programme or on small holdings where the veteran may derive his main income from employment apart from his holding.
With the brief statement that I have made of the vital principles of the bill, it may be desirable to explain its chief provisions in logical order. The desirabilty of such a measure, notwithstanding numerous failures which attended the Soldier Settlement Act, is strongly indicated by the expressed desire of substantial numbers of the members of the forces to engage in agricultural pursuits after the war. While our information about the intentions and desires of the members of the forces is not yet complete, sufficient information has been obtained to establish clearly that the number of men who wish to take up farming or to return to it will be very substantial. The demobilization committee of the government authorized a questionnaire to be addressed to all members of the forces with respect to their previous civil experience and training and their desires and ambitions for the future. The complete results of the questionnaire are not yet tabulated, so it is not possible as yet to indicate the precise number of men who have this desire. But a review of
200.000	of these forms indicates that 16-6 per cent of those completing the form had expressed the desire to settle on the land. This represents more than 33,000 individuals.
The following is a tabulation of the results obtained from an examination of more than
200.000	occupational history forms received and tabulated prior to October 31, 1941. It shows that in the navy, of a total of 17,588, those wishing to farm are 1,042 or 5-9 per cent. In the army the total examined numbered 136,913, and those wishing to farm are 29,067 or 21-2 per cent. In the air force the total number examined were 46,225, and

Veterans' Land Act
those wishing to farm are 3,343, or 7-1 per cent, making an over-all average at that time, among that number, of 16-6.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: Would those be mostly farm boys?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: Yes, in most instances they were. It is a hopeful and encouraging sign in connection with the proposed legislation that the desire to go on the land which is found among members of the forces serving in the present war does not seem to have any of those romantic illusions which captured the imagination of the soldiers of our generation twenty-five years ago. The men who have expressed a desire to take up farming, in the present instance at least, seem to be actuated by a sober, serious appreciation of what is involved. It is in keeping with the serious purpose of this measure that the director administering it is to be empowered to make regulations regarding the qualifications to be required of applicants. That is, it is expected that a loan shall not be issued unless the director is satisfied that the man has experience and ability which justify the expectation that he can make a success of farming.

speechtext:
Either they must have some experience or they must undergo a course of training, for which provision is made in the bill.
In regard to administration, the measure is to be administered by the Minister of Mines and Resources, through a director. Under the original Soldier Settlement Act, administration was placed in the hands of a statutory board. Later on, as hon. members are aware, that board was abolished and the administration was placed in the hands of one director. It has been deemed desirable to follow the latter practice in this instance. A board of three or more may be desirable where there are consultative features connected with the administration. Where, however, as in this measure, the administrative functions are not consultative but executive, it seems better that authority should be vested in one man, with the assistance of such technical advisers and staff as he may require.
I come now to the question of those who may be qualified. Those who qualify for assistance under this measure are confined to (1) members of the armed forces of Canada who served in a theatre of war; (2) members of the armed forces of Canada who did not serve in a theatre of war but who served for
