speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Yes; provided they were residents of Canada before the war, the same conditions apply. Provided an applicant has the above qualifications arising from military service, it shall be within the discretion of the director to determine whether or not he is entitled to be assisted; that is, on the grounds of qualification. Broadly speaking, the discretion of the director will be concerned with a man's fitness and qualifications for the vocation of agriculture. In cases where applicants are considered to require training, the director may make provision for placing veterans with selected farmers for practical instruction. Provision is also made for arriving at agreements with the federal and various provincial departments of agriculture, or the extension departments of Canadian universities, or accredited agricultural schools or colleges, for the purpose of training veterans.
The measure does not provide for subsistence during the training period, because the postdischarge order, administered by the Department of Pensions and National Health, contains provision for a scale of allowances to be paid to ex-service men whom it is considered can be helped toward reestablishment by vocational training. It is intended that the two departments shall cooperate in this connection. The director of the Veterans' Land Act will indicate the type of training required; and when subsistence for the individual applicant is needed, it will be forthcoming from the Department of Pensions and National Health under order in council P.C. 7633.
I come now to the powers of the director. The director is to have authority to buy or acquire land and farm property, which is to be vested in the director as a corporation sole. The land and property acquired by him shall be subject to taxation in the ordinary way by a properly constituted taxing authority. Under the old Soldier Settlement Act there was a period of uncertainty, which was ended only through costly and confusing litigation, as to whether soldier settlement lands should be subject to municipal taxation. In the present bill this issue is faced definitely from the outset, and it has been decided that the land shall pay taxes to the local authorities in exactly the same way as any other farm property.
Two types of transactions between the director and the veterans applying for assis-
Veterans' Land Act

tance are provided for in the measure. In one case the director buys the land and resells it to the veterans under agreement of sale, in accordance with the provisions of the bill. The director is required to calculate the cost price of any land acquired for the purpose of resale to veterans. In calculating the cost, he must take into account not only the price of the land but the cost of improvements effected under his own administration. A ceiling has been placed upon the cost which the director may incur in connection with any individual property; that ceiling is $4,800. This top limit is to include land and improvements, building materials, live stock and farm equipment. In connection with any individual transaction it is provided that the cost to the director of the land, improvements and building materials shall not exceed $3,600, out of the utmost price of $4,800. The veteran is required to make a cash down payment of ten per cent of the cost of the land, improvements and other materials. That is, if the property has cost the director the maximum amount, the veteran shall be required to pay down $360. It is provided that the live stock and farm equipment included in the transaction shall not exceed one-third of the cost to the director of the land, improvements and other materials. Again using the maximum figure, this means that if the land, improvements and building materials cost the director $3,600, the live stock and farm equipment shall not exceed $1,200. These two figures make up the ceiling cost of $4,800.
It is in the next provision that the government's grant to the settler is to be found. The sale price to the veteran of the complete enterprise, including live stock and farm equipment, shall be two-thirds of the cost to the director of the land, improvements and building materials. By way of illustration, if the land and improvements cost the director $3,600 and the. stock and implements cost the director $1,200, or a total of $4,800, then the indebtedness assumed by the veteran shall be $2,400, and the down payment to be made by the veteran shall be $360. The interest set out in the bill is 34 per cent, unless otherwise provided by the regulations. Payment shall be completed in a term of twenty-five years, with the interest calculated on an amortization basis. The director, however, may exercise his discretion to permit for the first five years the payment of interest only, but the total repayment period of twenty-five years is not to be exceeded.
No conveyance or transfer of the property shall be made to the veteran within the first ten years, and then only if the veteran has 
complied with the terms of his agreement. This means that the government's grant to the veteran is not made unless and until the veteran has proved by ten years' fulfilment of his contract that he is making good in his venture. While it is provided that the director shall not incur costs in excess of $4,800 upon any single property, there is nothing to debar a veteran from undertaking a larger venture if he is himself able out of his own resources to put up the additional amount of money required. In this connection it should be said that the proposed ceiling of $3,600 for the land is considered to be equivalent to the ceiling of $5,000 under the Soldier Settlement Act, having regard to present-day values.
I come now to the question of live stock and equipment. The Veterans' Land Act is so drafted that the veterans' land does not become encumbered with any charge or mortgage arising out of the acquisition of live stock and farm implements furnished to him by the director. The title in such live stock remains with the director until the time comes for disposal, when the director may facilitate marketing or exchange by conveying the ownership to the farmer.
In effect, live stock and equipment are merely issued to the farm and remain the property of the director until the ten-year period has elapsed, at the end of which the director may release the live stock and equipment to the veteran if he has complied with the terms of his agreement. This does not in any way militate against the farmer profiting from the sale of his live stock. Thus, increase from foundation stock may be sold and the proceeds used to meet farming expenses. It is expected, of course, that the value of foundation stock will be maintained.
The second type of assistance to settlers contemplated by the bill is a loan upon property which the veteran already owns. The amount of assistance, by way of loan, that may be made in these circumstances is limited to $3,200, and shall not exceed 60 per cent of the value of the land as established by the director.
Advances for the purpose of live stock and farm equipment shall not exceed 50 per cent of the value of the land, or a total of $2,500. Repayment may be extended over 25 years at the rate of 34 per cent.
It is felt that this provision may be of assistance to a number of veterans who have farms encumbered by mortgages at higher rates of interest than provided for in this measure.

Veterans' Land Act
It is considered that there may very well be cases in which a veteran possessed of a property worth from $6,000 to $10,000 may need a loan of only $2,000 to facilitate resumption of farming occupations. In cases, however, where the property is heavily encumbered, it is probable that the Veteran's Land Act will prove of greater assistance through outright purchase by the director and resale to the veteran on the terms contemplated by the provisions already described.
The bill provides that the veteran shall keep his property insured and that all taxes and assessments shall be paid, but there is a provision that, if the veteran is unable to pay taxes when they are due, the director may do so in his behalf and demand repayment with interest at 3i per cent.
One of the most important features of the bill is the method adopted for dealing with settlers who prove unsuccessful. Under the old Soldier Settlement Act, unsuccessful settlers clung to their land long after they should have given up the enterprise, and it was very difficult for the soldier settlement board to evict them, because from the very nature of the transaction it was exceedingly improbable that there could be any salvage to assist the settler in embarking upon any new enterprise.
The present bill gives the director definite powers of rescission when the veteran falls down on his payments. The director may, without resort to any legal proceedings, rescind the agreement and retake possession of the property. There is a requirement, however, that the director shall give thirty days' notice of intention by registered mail and, upon taking possession of the property, the director may sell, lease, or otherwise dispose of the property. Any surplus proceeds from the sale, over and above the outstanding costs and the expenses of the transaction, shall be paid to the veteran.
Before establishing any surplus, the director must take into account the cost to the director of all the property acquired for the veteran's establishment. Obviously this does not presuppose that veterans who fail will have established an equity in the enterprise. But there is provision in the bill to deal fairly with veterans who fail through ill health or other reasons beyond their control. If, in such cases, the director believes that no surplus will be realized upon resale, he may recommend to the minister, and the governor in council may, upon the minister's recommendation refund to the veteran his initial down ' payment in whole or in part.
In view of this, it is considered that the director will not be tempted to allow a veteran
to continue a doomed enterprise beyond the point at which his failure is indicated. The prompt application of the director's powers to rescind the agreement and the repayment to the veteran either of his down payment, or of a realized surplus upon resale of his property, will give the veteran an opportunity to reestablish himself in some other occupation where he is likely to have greater success than in farming. It is of no real assistance to the veteran who is doomed to failure to let him carry on for an unduly long period. It is far more in his interest that he shall cut his losses and try some other enterprise before he is too old to be able to make the change.
There are in the bill a number of miscellaneous provisions of considerable interest. It is obvious that the director will have to acquire a large amount of land, and, for its conservation pending sale to a veteran, the director is authorized to lease the property on terms approved by the minister. It is considered also that, in transactions of the magnitude of those upon which the director is authorized to embark, there will be a percentage of errors of judgment in valuation. Where such errors appear, there is a procedure whereby, under the approval of the minister, the property may be revalued or sold to others than veterans.
The director is also authorized to sell lands at his disposal as sites for dairy factories, cheese factories, fruit preserving factories, creameries, or for any educational, religious or charitable purposes. He may also sell lands to any provincial or municipal authorities for any purpose. Nobody indebted to the director of soldier settlement, under the Soldier Settlement Act, may receive a loan or advance under this measure.
A set of circumstances that arose not infrequently under the Soldier Settlement Act has been guarded against by a provision that the director may refuse to sell to a veteran land occupied by his parents or other immediate relatives. It was a not uncommon experience, under the Soldier Settlement Act that a father would sell his farm to the soldier settlement board for resale to his soldier son on the advantageous terms provided for in the Soldier Settlement Act. The result in many instances was that the father received a substantial sum of money from the soldier settlement board and remained in occupancy and management of the farm exactly as he was before. The soldier settler was thereby saddled with the maintenance of his father's family, as well as his own, and the whole transaction contributed nothing to the real problem of soldier settlement.
Veterans' Land Act

There is also very strict provision excluding commissions on the sale of land to the director. The prohibitions with regard to commissions are extensively set out in sections 32 and 33 of the bill, and severe penalties are prescribed. The bill provides for regulations to be made by the director for administrative purposes, and all regulations are required to be published in the Canada Gazette and tabled in parliament.
It has been estimated that under this bill an expenditure of $80,000,000 will provide for the settlement of 25,000 veterans. On that number of men, the capital loss arising from the provision for granting the veteran a percentage of his equity, would be $34,000,000. This is an average of $1,360 per settler. The capital loss per case under the old act was an average of $4,000, which represents the concessions granted from time to time.
It will interest the committee to know that this bill is the result of more than a year's study and consideration by one of the committees set up under the cabinet committee on demobilization and reestablishment. The cabinet committee, it will be remembered, is advised by a general advisory committee, presided over by the chairman of the Canadian pension commission, and consisting of senior officers of eight or ten government departments.
The general advisory committee, in turn, set up a series of subcommittees to deal with specialized phases of the problem of reestablishment. One of these committees was assigned the subject of soldier settlement, and the present bill is the product of its labours. Advice and assistance were received not only from government officials, but from a number of authorities outside the service of the dominion government. Some of the most prominent citizens of Canada were engaged in that work for eighteen months, before the bill was finally approved by the government.
The members of this committee and its consultants and advisers are entitled to the thanks of the government and of this house for the measure which is to be presented to the house, after the adoption of the resolution.
In conclusion, I would commend the measure to the earnest consideration of the special committee, and afterwards, of the house.

Would the minister go a little more fully into the matter of the judgment of the director in connection with settling a veteran on the land? I can contemplate a condition where a great number of young men who left agriculture at a very young age have spent three or four years overseas. They will come back without a firm foundation of agricultural knowledge. Let us assume that a young man has satisfied the director that he is a fit and proper person to return to the farm. Would it not be in the public interest, either by a course of training or instruction, to see that this man was given the necessary training in farm pursuits? I think the minister realizes that farming today is not what it was in the days of the last war. It is a much more technical pursuit, requiring more skilled management in carrying it out. After this
war is over, it will probably be much more so. I think the utmost care will have to be taken in seeing that these young men are given the proper training. The veteran who has dreamed of a utopia on the land is quite likely to find a different condition existing upon his return; and if he is not given the proper training before being placed on the land, his chances of success may be lessened.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
I doubt if there is a
subject which could come before the committee where the personal equation enters more into the picture than it does in this matter of soldier land settlement. I should like to point out to the minister in charge that I have a great sympathy with him because of the problem which he is attempt. ing to meet with this proposed legislation. Those who have made some study of the problems which successive governments have had to solve in connection with land settlement since the last war will realize the problem which now confronts this administration. But I do submit that in dealing with the question of veterans' land settlement the whole matter of the disparity between agricultural returns and those from other industries in the dominion must inevitably be
Veterans' Land Act

taken into consideration and must inevitably form a factor as to whether this scheme shall be a success or a failure.
I can conceive of the difficulties encountered by any person going on the land. I can still recall most vividly the difficulties my own father experienced through the years in trying to wipe out debt on his agricultural lands. It meant not only hard work but long hours and the saving of every possible penny of farm income. For that reason it seems to me that the committee must take into consideration the necessity of bringing the man on the farm up to a position of economic equality with other classes in this dominion. It is all very well to give our soldiers who are demobilized from active service after the war every possible advantage to start with, but something more is needed to keep them on the land after they get there, as well as those already on the land who have now a stake in agriculture. Most of the farmers with whom I have talked are of the opinion that it is almost impossible in many parts of Canada to-day for a man to make ends meet, if he has to pay interest upon any considerable portion of his investment.
I think we all realize that the difference between success and failure on the land, whether the farmer be a soldier or a civilian, is quite often a matter of how much interest he has to pay on the debt owing on his farm and the amount of principal he has to repay. So it seems to me that in this soldier settlement plan which has been outlined by the minister we must first of all bring agriculture up to a parity with other lines of activity in our economic life. Not only must we encourage these men to produce the stuff, but we must help them find a market for it at a proper price after it is produced. I can conceive of nothing more pathetic than to bring a man who has been demobilized from active service into any industry which has not at least an equal chance of success with other lines of activity.
May I say this too, from a practical point of view. The question of the adaptability of the man who is to go on the farm is of major importance and must never be lost sight of in the administration of this measure.
There are many people who think they would like to farm, but the desire to farm and the ability to make a success of it, are two different matters, and we have had thousands of cases across this dominion to show7 that the adaptability of the individual is a most important factor. Then there is, of course, an angle which the bachelor Minister of Pensions and National Health could not be

expected to appreciate. From my experience in agriculture-and this is no reflection on the menfolk on the farms-I w'ould say: Show me a good farmer's wife and I will show you a good farmer. The womenfolk are a very important factor in the success of anyone who settles on the land, no matter where he may be.
May I say, in closing, that the director of this project and the board that is to be set up will need to do much more than take just simply a business administrative interest in these settlers. They will need to exercise a fatherly supervising eye over the men who go on the land. Some of the most glaring failures in land settlement under previous administrations have been largely attributable to the fact that men were placed on the land, given an opportunity that looked good on paper, and then afterwards there was no supervision, no fatherly eye was kept upon them by those in authority or even by their neighbours. The director himself ought not to be just an ordinary civil servant, and I am making no reflection on the service when I say that, because the thought I have in mind is that the director of this land settlement scheme must be first of all a man who has made his own money by the sweat of his brow on a dirt farm. I do not care whether he is a prominent citizen of Canada or not. I am more interested in getting a man who knows the farm problem intimately so that he will understand what the settlers will face when they go on the land. Certainly he should be a veteran of the last war and, if possible, a man who has undertaken and made a success, if you will, of farm settlement under some scheme administered by previous governments. He should have associated with him men of broad, practical farming experience.
I want to say this to the committee, that so far we have only scratched the surface in giving agriculture adequate representation on the many boards which have been appointed in this country in connection with our war effort. We should not be ashamed to put farmers upon every board in the country. If we had had more farmers on boards in Canada in the last twenty-five years, certainly we would have had less extravagance and better management than we have had on many public boards in this dominion.

speechtext:
-tout I am told they belong for the most part to the professions. The board to be appointed must never lose sight of the advantage of having the advice of practical farmers who understand what it means for a man and his wife to go on a soldier settlement farm to carve out what may prove to be a very precarious living. The committee, then, it seems to me, should give consideration, first of all, to the adaptability of the men who are to go on the land; next, sympathetic supervision should be exercised over them; and equally important, there should be something like equality of opportunity with other lines in our economic life. In other words, our farmers should have' a parity of return, the opportunity of being on an equal basis with other lines in our economic life.
Mr. QUE.LCH: I find myself thoroughly in accord with the sentiments which have just been expressed by the hon. member for Peel. I do not feel any too optimistic about the chances of the soldier's success under this land settlement scheme. Any soldier who starts with a debt of $3,600 on a half- or quarter-section of land and has to farm under an agricultural policy such as we had in this country from 1930 to 1939, will find that he has an impossible task on his hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: My hon. friend referred to a maximum debt of $3,600. The maximum debt will be $2,400.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Even with a debt of $2,000 on a quarter- or half-section of land, the soldier will find he has an impossible task on his hands under the type of agricultural policy that we -had in this country from 1930 to 1939, because during that period, year after year, the farmers had to sell their products 'below the cost of production. Show me any concern that continues to produce below the cost of production, and I will show you a concern that is going to go into debt. Before considering any new land settlement scheme, the government would be well advised to take the necessary steps to clean up the old one- and that old scheme needs a good deal of cleaning up at the present time.
In order to judge of the principle of this new -bill, we should have a thorough understanding of the land settlement act -that was brought in at the end of the last war. Then, perhaps, we shall be in -a better position to avoid the tragic mistakes which were made under that one. The story of settlement under the last scheme is one of tragedy and despair, interspersed all too infrequently with happy memories or records of success. I want to stress to the minister the all-important fact
that unless a more humane attitude is adopted towards many of those men who still remain under the scheme, the closing chapters of that story are indeed going to be sordid ones. Since the government has undoubtedly a very direct responsibility for the conditions which exist under -that scheme, I think they should take immediate steps to rectify them.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health dealt to a certain extent with the former scheme, but on the other hand there are many angles with which he did not deal. He did not refer at any length to the tragic conditions which exist under that scheme as a result of the policy laid down by the government.
Some of the main reasons for this unhappy picture may be briefly summarized as follows:
In the first place the method of selecting settlers was a haphazard one. Many of the soldiers regarded the scheme as just another adventure. They were neither physically nor mentally equipped for the job. The majority of them in the early stages of the scheme gave up. Then, many settlers-and the same will happen after this war-brought back young wives from the old country, girls who had lived a decent, simple country life; and these girls were called upon to live in such squalor and poverty that, in a great many instances, they refused to stay on the land. In some instances the family left the land; in others, domestic troubles ensued and the families were broken up. In either event that was the end of the soldier as a settler. In many instances the choice of supervisor was unfortunate. Men were chosen who had no qualifications for the job. Poor land was purchased as well as inferior stock and equipment. The soldier settler was exploited from every side. For some reason or another the soldier settler after the last war was looked upon as fair game for exploitation, and unfortunately the supervisor too often was not qualified to give him the protection which he needed. Purchases were made while prices were greatly inflated. Any old cows were selling at $125 each, and equivalent peak prices obtained for other kinds of stock. Land prices were based on $2 a bushel wheat. Consequently the settler had to face an interestbearing debt which he could not possibly meet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member a question? Would he not say that the greatest cause of the failure of farmers under the scheme of the last war was inflation, the inflation at the end of the war?
Veterans' Land Act

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: Undoubtedly inflation was one of the causes, but I would not say that it was the main cause. I would point out to the minister that even the civilian farmers, who had benefited by inflation, found themselves in tragic circumstances afterwards. The distress was not confined to the soldier settler. If the civilian farmer twenty years after the war found himself in a position of bankruptcy, how much more likely was it that the soldier settler would be in a no less difficult position? To a certain extent, of course, inflation exists at present. If you compare prices of stock before the war with prices to-day, you might say that to-day's prices are highly inflated, or rather that the price of stock before the war was greatly deflated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I was just trying to be helpful; that is all. I think that shows the tremendous importance of preventing inflation now and at the end of this war, because it was the high prices which were paid for farms and for stock by these soldier settlers which weighed them down and kept them in misery for a decade or more and eventually ruined a great many.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: Would the minister say that prices of stock to-day are not inflated? If that is the situation, would he guarantee that the prices which are now received for stock will be continued after the war? Can he guarantee that five years after the war the price of cattle will not be half what it is to-day? I do not think he would consider for one minute doing so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I cannot guarantee anything of that kind but I will guarantee that I will do everything within my power, and the government will do all it can, to prevent the kind of inflation which set in after the last war.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: What about the deflation which will set in?

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I believe the farmer will be more interested if the government will guarantee that the condition of deflation which we had in this country from 1930 to 1939 will not be allowed to come again. It is all very well to talk about inflation but speaking generally the farmer benefits as a result of inflation; it is deflation against which he wishes to be protected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I am not talking about these soldier settlers buying farms during a period of deflation.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Unfortunately they were victims of something which was far worse than that. I know many soldier settlers and civilian farmers who in 1928 were fairly well off who had a fair amount of money in the bank a paid-up insurance policy and no mortgage, but who at the beginning of the present war were bankrupt. It was this continued deflationary policy which, along with drought, ruined the farmers. I know many who did not suffer from drought who were ruined by low prices. No farmer can continue year after year to produce crops and stock below the cost of production and continue in business. Once his reserves are gone, he is forced into debt. We all know that was the position of agriculture. Of course, any farmer who has to start in during an inflationary period is under a still greater handicap.
Another big mistake which was made was that many soldier settlers were placed on marginal land, and in a drought area. The constituency I represent comprises a great part of the drought area of Alberta. Many soldier settlers were placed in that area, in spite of the fact that the government had been warned year after year by their engineers and surveyors that that land was not suitable for the purpose. Just to show the type of land to which I refer, eight million acres have been taken back by the provincial government, who are now leasing, in many instances three thousand acres to each farmer, realizing that it takes that amount of land to enable him to make a living. Yet soldier settlers were put in that area on a halfsection or a quarter-section basis. What possible chance had those men of making a success? They were settled under the advice and supervision of the soldier settlement board. All expenditures had to be passed by the board for payment. Therefore, I think, the federal government assumed a very direct responsibility for what took place.
The minister gave some figures of the number of settlers who went on the land and the number who are left. I want to quote another set of figures. To-day, approximately twenty-three years after the initiation of the scheme, out of a total of twenty-five thousand established under the act, only 7,360 remain under the scheme. Of course that does not mean that all of the 17,640 can be classified as failures. I believe that three thousand of them have paid in full for their land, but undoubtedly the majority of these men must be looked upon as failures. I want to break down that 7,360. Of the 7,360 who still remain under the scheme, 2,953 have an average equity of 67-5 per cent; 606 have an average equity

Veterans' Land Act
of 32 per cent, 1,078 have an average equity of 16 per cent, and 2,723 have absolutely no equity of any kind. So, out of the total of 7,360, 3,801, or 52 per cent, have an equity of less than 16 per cent. In other words, 52 per cent of the soldier settlers who are still under the scheme have no chance of ever making a success. I say that for this reason. I want to quote figures which were given to the special committee on pensions last year by Mr. Walter Woods. I will quote what he stated at the time, as reported at page 768 of the record:
Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, I understand that this morning I am required to make some comment on the deliberations of a subcommittee of the general advisory committee that has been dealing with the subject of land settlement for the new forces.
He goes on:
It is perhaps sufficient to say that the committee finds itself in agreement on certain important principles, the outstanding one of which is that state financial assistance, a substantial part of which will not be recoverable, is a prerequisite to the institution of any comprehensive plan of land settlement as a rehabilitation measure.
This is the important point to which I wish to call attention:
The question arises as to what is a safe margin. What equity should a settler have to ensure reasonable chances of success? Private mortgage companies have set a limit of approximately 50 per cent. The Canadian farm loan board has a limit of 50 per cent. The Central Mortgage Bank Act contemplates reducing the farmer's total debt for land and equipment to 80 per cent.
You will notice that the private mortgage companies figure that a soldier must have an equity of at least 50 per cent in the land; yet to-day, under the land settlement scheme, there are 3,801 men who have an equity of less than 16 per cent. In other words, we are justified in saying that at least 52 per cent of the men who are still under the scheme have little or no chance of succeeding. What is to become of these men? The majority of the 3,801 have come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act; but unfortunately, owing to continued crop failures and low prices, they have lost all the benefits of their reductions. But even if they were young, even if their equipment were in good shape, those men would not have any chance of succeeding, judging from the figures given to the committee by Mr. Woods. Unfortunately, however, they are no longer young. The majority of them are getting on in age. Their stock and equipment are old and their buildings are dilapidated. To-day these men are being pressed-I think I am almost justified in saying that they are being houndedby the soldier settlement board. I am not criticizing the board for their action because they are only carrying out a policy imposed upon them. Let me read a letter from the British Empire Service League on a very important question-rather, it is not a letter but the report of a soldiers' committee. It is the report of the soldiers' settlers committee of the legion.
Your committee begs to report as follows:
Since being appointed at a meeting of the provincial council held in the Memorial hall, Edmonton, on January 2nd of this year, to investigate soldier settlers' affairs, I have received from the provincial secretary copies of the resolutions dealing with soldier settlers; and I have written the branch sponsoring the resolution, asking for statutory declarations to substantiate the claims set forth in their resolutions.
I have had sufficient replies with the required evidence to prove that all is not well with our comrades, the soldier settlers, and it is my considered opinion that many of them are struggling under a load of debt too great for them to carry. I find from the evidence submitted that the S.S.B. has been insistent on the yearly payments being met regardless of whether there was enough left over to insure a living for the settler or not.
In many cases where the soldier settler was dispossessed, the land was sold later to other parties, who were not ex-service men, for a great deal less money than the debt of the original settler for the board amounted to. It is possible that if the board had given the soldier settler the same price as the land was sold for he might have been able to carry on and remain in possession of his land.
I have also seen letters myself written by the board to soldier settlers informing them that in view of the fact that they were in the position where they could not pay for the land, they might as well get off it. I would ask, where are these men to go? They are told that they have no chance of succeeding now and that they have no equity. Where will they go if they are forced off the land? Men of that age cannot easily find a job, and many of them are physically incapable of working. Of that total only 554 are receiving war veterans' allowance. I would say that as part of our war effort immediate steps should be taken to investigate the situation in regard to these 3,801 men to whom I have referred, before initiating any new scheme, I think it is the obligation of the government to take the necessary steps to reestablish those men who are already on the land. I have absolutely no faith that under the new scheme conditions in the long run will be any better than they are under this one, unless the government can guarantee an agricultural policy for the future which will return to the farmers cost of production. I would recommend that where there is a chance of a settler

Veterans' Land Act

carrying on, especially where he has the help of his children, the amount of the debt should be written down to a point where he will be in a position to pay it. I say to the government, treat him the same as you are treating the soldiers of this war. Treat him the same as he should have been treated under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Owing to the continuance of low prices, the farmer now finds himself no better off than when his debts were reduced under that act.
Unfortunately the board have no power to reduce these debts to the point I suggest. Legislation is necessary to make it possible. I have spoken to officials of the board, and I found that they would have been only too glad to make a reduction, but they had no power. They could only suggest that where the settler was married, he should release the farm so as to enable his wife to buy it from the board. They would be then in a position to sell it to her at a greatly reduced figure. Why they had to deal with the subject in that roundabout way I do not know, but not all settlers have wives, and it can be done only where there is a wife. On the other hand, where the disability or the ill-health of the soldier prevents his ever making a success of the farm, even if the debt were reduced, I would urge on the government that they carry on a somewhat similar scheme for such men as they propose under the new measure. They should place these men in communities, in low rental cottages, with decent gardens, and pay them a war veterans' allowance so that they can at least finish their days in a certain amount of peace.
Let me refer to one thing more, a certain action on the part of this government which I regard as despicable. I would not have believed that this government could possibly be guilty of such an action if the evidence had not been presented to me. The government passed an order in council which gave them power to seize a portion of dependent's allowance in payment of the soldier settler's debt. When that matter was first called to my attention I told the particular settler, "You must be wrong, because under the regulations dependent's allowances cannot be touched." He replied, "I don't know whether they can or cannot be touched, but the point is that they are being seized at the present time."
When I got here I took the matter up with the board and found that order in council P.C. 138, 1936, had been passed. Perhaps I should read that order in council because there are not very many people who are familiar with it. I hope the minister is not

proud of his responsibility for this order in council.
The board has had under consideration a submission of the honourable the Minister of Mines and Resources reporting that:
1.	A considerable number of persons who agreed to purchase farms from the soldier settlement board or from the director of soldier settlement on long term contracts have enlisted in the Canadian armed forces.
2.	In many cases the dependents of such enlisted persons continue to occupy their farms but no provision has been made for payment of instalments in respect of their contracts or of taxes in respect of their farms.
3.	The director of soldier settlement has no authority to carry such accounts indefinitely and it is considered desirable to provide for deductions from dependents' allowances to cover local taxes and interest due.
Accordingly the board recommend that notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained in any of the regulations providing for payment of dependents' or marriage allowances in respect of dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces, that in all cases where the dependents of an enlisted person continue to occupy the farm for which such person is indebted to the director of soldier settlement and in respect of which the contract terms are not otherwise satisfactorily provided for, there may be deducted from the dependents' or marriage allowance amounts sufficient to provide for payment of taxes levied by the local taxing authority in respect of the property in question and interest accruing annually on indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement, such deductions to be made monthly and in no case to exceed $20 per month except with the consent of the dependents concerned.
After having read this, I wrote the settler asking if he would forward me the correspondence that had taken place between himself and the board with regard to this matter. A number of cases were brought to my attention, but I am going to refer only to one specific case. First, I should like to read the letter which the soldier settler received from the board, without giving the name:
We have for acknowledgment your letter of September 26 requesting that we consider cancelling the deduction from your dependents' allowance of $13 a month under P.C. 138/1936.
Before it is possible for us to make any recommendation in this connection to head office it must be ascertained what amount will be received from the crop proceeds to apply against the contract.
You no doubt realize the state of your husband's account. The current loan instalment amounts to $126.36 with arrears outstanding of $355.65 making a total due on October 1 of $482.01. To date, against this sum we have only received $73.89.
When your husband's account was adjusted under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act the board of review ordered that in each year the department should receive a one-fourth share of all crops grown on this land as collateral to the payment called for annually but this, of course, is not the basis of the

Veterans' Land, Act
settlement. In other words, if the crop share does not meet the annual payment, Mr. . . . is required to make up the difference.
According to the information we have re-. ceived, the one-fourth share of the crop this year will in no way meet the equivalent of an annual instalment nor will it even amount to the carrying charges.
We must, therefore, leave this matter in abeyance for the time being.
You will notice that according to the agreement under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, this settler had to turn over one-quarter of his crop, but that did not meet the payment, so they were deducting $13 a month from the dependents' allowance.

It does not. This man had a number of children, but at that time they were given allowances for only two children, so it could not have been more than $35 plus the allowance for the two children. I took up this matter with the board, who finally agreed to refund the amount of money that this woman had paid out of the crop proceeds, under the agreement, but they refused to stop this seizure of a portion of the dependents' allowance. I suggested that it would be better for them to insist upon the turning over of one-quarter of the crop, and allow this woman to keep the dependents' allowance. Their reply, however, was "No, we will not do that, for this reason. She may not always get a crop. If we just insist on a quarter share of the crop we may get nothing, but if we deduct a share of the dependents' allowance we will get that right along." In other words, they were destroying the very principle laid down by the dependents' allowance regulations, of which section 98 reads:
A dependent's allowance may not be claimed as a right. The allowance is for the purpose of promoting the well-being and efficiency of the military forces of Canada by providing a means to alleviate the financial anxieties of temporarily enrolled members with respect to the domestic welfare of dependents. . . .
Note that; it is for the purpose of removing anxiety from the mind of the soldier; yet the soldier settlement board refuses to accept a part of the crop, insisting upon a portion of the dependents' allowance because they do not want any financial anxiety. They prefer to place that anxiety upon the soldier, though it was the purpose of these regulations to remove it.

If the government is going to seize a portion of the dependents' allowance, this woman will not have the money with which to pay this man. During the winter, because of the health of

the children and the distance to school, she has to move into town and pay rent. The only excuse given by the board in this case was that they were merely charging a fair rental for the use of the farm property. If that is true, I would ask this question. If a soldier owns a house, does the board deduct from the dependents' allowance in that case an amount equal to the rent for that building? Certainly it does not. Then, why should it be deducted in the case of a person on the land, who is far less able to pay? If the government are justified in this action, a mortgage company would be equally justified in asking the government to allow it to seize a certain proportion of a dependents' allowance as fair rent for property on which they have a mortgage. Why should the government take unto itself the right to do something that no one else can do? I think, as I said before, that this is a most despicable action.

Yes. In spite of this, there is a capital loss to the settlement board averaging about $4,000 on an original debt of $4,400 to $4,600. The cost of collection runs about 40 per cent. We would have been a good deal further ahead if we had given them the land, to start with. We would have had about 25,000 noble veterans of the last war who would have had homes. But the net result of what has happened is that only 10 per cent of these men have been able to pay off their indebtedness, in spite of the fact that settlers altogether have paid $65,000,000. Two-thirds of these noble veterans have given up in despair.
Where are they to-day? The 33 per cent who do remain on their homes are, in many instances, living in miserable hovels. They are living in fear and in insecurity. They are wondering when the representatives of the soldier settlement board will be around to ask them to give up everything, to sign a quitclaim deed and get off the land. Those veterans are now twenty years older than when they returned from the last war, when they were willing to give their lives for this land of ours. Now their home is tied down to debt -to inflation, as the Minister of Finance has said. Interest is bled out of these people on that debt.
As the previous speaker -has pointed out, the government is apparently out-Shylocking Shylock in passing orders in council compelling the wives of these men to take certain action. If the settler enlists again, in many instances to obtain a living, she is forced by order in council, to give up a portion of her separation allowance. In many instances these returned veterans are only wrecks of their former selves. Surely it should be the intention of such a bill to provide homes for those men who were willing to sacrifice. If that is so, then in heaven's name remove some of the worry and insecurity and fear that fill the hearts of these people. Give them a chance to make homes for themselves. Is that not the intention?

Whose cost? If it is 50 per cent of something valued at twice what it is worth, what is the difference? In the .years those men spent on the land they have given all their labour, and the labour of their wives and families to produce some cash return, something to maintain their home. They are forced to pay their taxes; those must be paid. In this instance the board is going to lend that money to pay the taxes, and pile that on top of the soldier's indebtedness.
Then, every year the capital debt against each man is going to reap its interest. True, the interest rate is lower than it was last time. Still it is too great, because in all those years when there was no return for a farmer's work his labour went for nothing; but the capital invested there has to be paid its interest; the debt must reap its reward. Oh, yes, capital has to have its reward, -whether labour is paid or not!
The second suggestion made by the hon. member for Acadia was that something should be done under the bill to provide decent homes for these people. Something should be done to see that men going into this scheme are not tied down to burdens too great for them to carry. Something should be done for those men who are already trying to hang on, on present settlement board farms throughout the country. If for 20 years these men have continued on those farms; if they have worked for 20 years and have stuck to their jobs, surely those men and their wives and families, after what they have suffered as a result of the last war, should receive better treatment. Surely, for the balance of their worried lives they should be told, "Well, you have done your bit. At least there is a home for you for the rest of your days." Instead of that, they are being hounded and asked to pay interest and payments, year after year.
I received a letter from one of them who happens to live in my constituency. His income will not be any more than $300 cash for the whole year. He has paid his taxes this year. He informed the supervisor that his wife had contracted a cancer, and that she had been in hospital for about seven weeks. The supervisor was informed that the wife would have to return to the hospital every two months, but no account was taken of that. On the contrary he received a letter from the provincial office telling him they would like to receive $15 or $20 as a token payment, to keep the debt in good standing.
This type of thing-well, I claim it is almost sabotage, in days like these. Some better ray of hope than what is shown in this bill will have to be placed before them. The
treatment of these men has been dastardly, and I do not see much hope in this bill unless there is a change of viewpoint.
The purpose of the bill should be that of providing homes, with security. Assuming that a farm in an ordinary year should make a certain return, then I would say in such case a settler could make a payment, and I believe he would be willing to. But in those years when there are no returns for work, there should be no interest piled on-none at all. Weather conditions, crop conditions, price conditions, and market conditions vary from year to year. These are matters over which the farmer has no control. But, in spite of the fact that he is prevented from earning anything, extra debt is placed upon him. This should not be.

speechtext:
I did not interrupt the hon. member, and I ask him to keep his place now. When he says the treatment accorded by the government to the men who returned from the last war was dastardly, I throw it back in his teeth, and tell him he does not know what he is talking about.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health gave a summary of the benefits or readjustments made on behalf of the returned men who settled on the land after the last war. There is no doubt that there were many who settled at that time who should not have done so. But they expressed a preference to gO' to the land, and their preference was met.
I cannot agree either with the hon. member for Acadia. I do not know whether these two hon. gentlemen are in favour of the principle of the bill, or are opposed to it. I would judge from their remarks that they are opposed, and that they do not wish to see the government make any provision for the settlement on land of the men who will come back from the present war. If they are in favour of the bill, why do they not rise in their places and say so?
The hon. member for Acadia painted a rather gloomy picture of the last land settlement scheme. I admit that there were difficulties. The scheme was new when ii was undertaken-I may tell the committee that
17S4
Veterans' Land Act

I did not have any responsibility for that scheme-it was a new venture altogether in land settlement. There is no doubt that high prices were paid for the land because, as the Minister of Finance stated1 a moment ago, it was bought at a time of highly inflated values. The scheme came into effect and was operative in the latter part of 1919, and in 1920 and 1921, before deflation in values took place. It was during those years that a large amount of the land upon which these men were settled was purchased, and unquestionably it was purchased at inflated values. That was recognized by the several adjustments that were made from time to time. I would say that that was the first difficulty in the last scheme.
The next difficulty was that no test was madfe of the men who were settled on the land; that is, no test of their experience in a practical way to manage and operate farms. I think I am within the judgment of those in the house who are familiar with farming operations when I say that to succeed on a farm a man needs some experience and the ability to apply managerial skill; he must have the ability to apply those qualities that lead to success in any occupation. The old-fashioned idea was-perhaps it entered too much into the last scheme-that the main requisite for a farmer was a strong back. That is not the situation. If a man is going to succeed in farming, he must possess managerial skill, experience and the knowledge of how to make the best of the occupation he is in. Without discrediting any of the returned men from the last war, I think it is admitted) that many of them did not have that experience. Indeed, some of them had never been on a farm in their lives, at least had not done any practical work, and naturally they were handicapped. That was a serious handicap.
In many instances men were settled on poor land. I am not going to criticize the methods by which the land settlement scheme was carried through; but I know that in my own province, in the area between lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba, the land is not good farming land, and yet many soldier settlers were placed there. They were handicapped from the beginning by that very fact. These have been guarded against in the measure which the Minister of Pensions and National Health introduced to the house this evening. There is provision for the selection of suitable land; there is provision that experienced men only are to be placed on the land. If an individual has not had farming experience, an opportunity is to be given

to him to acquire that experience in a practical way before he undertakes the job of managing his own farm.

Provision is made also for much more generous assistance on the part of the government than was given under the last scheme. With the experience gained in the operation of the soldier land settlement scheme, there is a reasonable chance-I would say a good chance-that in the great majority of cases this scheme will succeed.
The last scheme vras not quite the dreary failure indicated in the remarks made a short time ago by the hon. member for Acadia. There were between 24,000 and 25,000 settlers placed upon the land.

According to the last census figures, there are to-day over 70,000 farms in Canada occupied by farmers over sixty-five years of age with no grown sons to follow them. All the time farms of that kind are coming into the market. Let me repeat:	I do not think

Mr. Chairman, I ask your indulgence because I realize that I am out of order, but I do not want to let the statement made by the hon. member for Acadia pass without some qualifications. He gave an instance of a veteran of the last war who had enlisted in this war, leaving his wife and several children on the farm. He criticized the government severely because it had asked that a certain amount, I believe it was $13 a month, should be given by the recipient of the allowance toward paying taxes and maintaining interest payments on the farm. There are cases of that kind.
I think that was the kind of case to which the hon. member for Yorkton applied the adjective "dastardly". What were the circumstances of the case? In the first place, the wife of the soldier got an allowance of $35 a month contingent upon his assigning $20 of his pay each month. For each of two children she got an allowance of $12 a month. Therefore altogether she was in receipt of $79 a month. She was not disturbed in her possession of the farm; she could rent it or work it herself, and pay a quarter of the proceeds to the soldier settlement board. She was asked to pay $13 a month for taxes and to help pay the interest on the amount that was owing. That is the treatment to which the hon. member for Yorkton applies the adjective "dastardly". I think it would require a pretty good stretch of the imagination for anyone to consider that dastardly treatment.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I was not referring merely to that. It seemed to me dastardly that the government would take unto itself powers which were not permitted even to a mortgage company.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT

speechtext:
I have as Minister of Mines and Resources charge of the administration of the Soldier Land Settlement Act. I invite the hon. member for Yorkton and any other hon. member to give me chapter and verse of the particulars of any case, and I am quite willing to submit them to the judgment of
the house. There may have been cases-I do not say there were none, although I would be surprised if I found any-where some hardship has resulted, but the whole purpose of the government in administering this scheme was not to oppress the settlers but to help them put their properties in a position where they -would have a secure home for themselves for the future. There have been cases where $50, $60, $75 and, in some instances, $79 a month have been paid to soldier's dependents on the farm, where a veteran of the last war has enlisted in this war. That is a fair sum, $75 a month, when you are living on a farm where you have a home to live in and security of tenure. You are not paying rent. You are paying a part of the proceeds-in the particular case cited by the hon. member for Acadia, a quarter of the proceeds-but it is in the interests of the veteran himself and in the interests of the home to pay the taxes. Therefore I hope the hon. member for Yorkton will, upon reflection, conclude that the administration of the scheme is not nearly so severe as he would have the members of the committee believe.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: In the riding of the Minister of Mines and Resources I was driven over a large territory just west of the Pas. It is some of the finest land in the world, open for settlement, and is available at a very low price. I would think it would be a splendid piece of land to settle anybody upon. Again, north of the Peace river I was shown very large areas of land upon which no one was residing. I do not see why the government could not settle large numbers of men in blocks up there. I have also in mind what is being done for the Sudetens. The Minister of Mines and Resources is more familiar with that than I am, although I spent some time in that territory upon two occasions.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: If I may interject, all the provinces of Canada have been approached and have indicated their utmost desire to cooperate by way of surveys and otherwise in order to make the scheme a success.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
What I had in mind was that if large blocks of good land were available here and there at a very low price, it would be much better to settle the soldiers upon such land than upon land which was heavily encumbered with debt from the very beginning. Land settlement after a war is not a new thing. After the Revolutionary war, the United Empire Loyalists were settled in Canada in the eastern counties and the counties just west of Kingston, in Frontenac and Hastings. After the war of 1812, large numbers of soldiers were settled in Lanark county. They were given the land free, obtaining title to it after being upon it for three years. They were also given various implements with which to work the land, and were given rations for two years if they were required; and as I read history, most of these settlers made good. Many of my people on my father's side were soldiers of the Napoleonic wars, and they settled in Lanark county and made good. A private drew 100 acres; a lieutenant and a captain, larger amounts respectively. They made good partly because they were not encumbered with debt from the very beginning.
I have listened with interest to what has been said by hon. gentlemen from the west who sit to my left, who are familiar with the problems of the soldier settlers in the west; and after listening to what they have said it would appear to me that one of the reasons why some of these soldier settlers failed to make good is that they were encumbered with debt from the beginning. On the other hand, I believe that what the Minister of Finance has said is largely true, that infla-

tion after the last war had a lot to do with the lack of success of many of these settlers.
I should like to see the bill contain provisions whereby the soldier settlers will be able to start on the land with a very low encumbrance of debt, if any at all. I would rather see them start free of debt, because I agree with what one hon. member to my left has said that if they are given the land free and they make good, that is to the advantage of Canada, and is much better than to settle the soldiers upon land encumbered with debt which they would give up after working upon it for a few years.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
May I ask a question of the Minister of Mines and Resources arising out of statements made by some hon. members and the minister's answer with respect to deductions from dependents' allowances. I shall be more moderate in what I say than the hon. member for Yorkton, but that, of course, is no reflection upon him. I should like to ask the government to review its position with regard to deduction from dependents' allowances, upon two grounds. First of all, in making the deduction the government is putting into operation a principle which is denied to private individuals. My understanding of the provisions is that no dependent's allowance can be garnisheed. It is judgment-proof. My understanding of the dependents' allowance provision is that they may not be garnisheed; they are judgment-proof, and in addition to that, the ordinary operations of law do not apply to the soldiers dependents' allowance. It seems to me, if that is the situation-and I am going on that assumption- the government is going a long way when it attempts to meet any governmental payment out of the dependents' allowance. The money is given to the dependents of soldiers serving in this war.
Might I also advance this suggestion? You are dealing here with veterans of two wars. You are dealing with the family of the man who served in the last war, and you are dealing wdth the same family where the head of that family is serving in this war. It seems to me that, if any evidence were really necessary on which to base a request to the government to review the situation again, this latter argument ought to hold water.
If the minister cares to reply, I should like some information, or at least an estimate, with regard to how many soldier settlers there are whose wives or dependents are being asked from time to time to share some of the burden out of their dependents' allowances.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
I have the information here. There are 297 deductions being made.

Veterans' Land Act
Of these, 260 voluntarily asked that the reductions be made. My hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health, who has a mathematical turn, tells me that that constitutes 87J per cent. Within the total are only thirty-seven cases which might come within the strictures made by the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for York-ton. These 260 people see the desirability and advantage of making a contribution from their allowances; they are interested in ultimately owning their homes and protecting them; and we give them every encouragement possible. Unfortunately all human beings are not made alike; all soldier settlers are not alike; but I venture to say that every one of those thirty-seven cases would be found to be within the category where they can well afford without hardship to make a contribution towards keeping their homes in good standing. I do not think it is any imposition to ask them to do it. If hon. members are interested in the matter, when the soldier settlement estimates are before the house at a later period I shall be glad to give particulars of every case and to leave it to the judgment of the house whether, in the words of the hon. member for Yorkton, they are being used in a "dastardly" fashion.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I understand that 260 are described as voluntary. Am I not correct in assuming that they were asked if they would voluntarily give this contribution? In certain cases they were.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I am not entering into this discussion, because I think we are wasting time in talking this evening about after-war problems instead of preparing to win the war, but I do not think it is fair to speak of this as purely voluntary. I have seen some of these letters, and I would not call the arrangement exactly voluntary.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT

Did the committee who recommended the plan embodied in this bill, or did the government, give any consideration to settling these soldiers, when they return, in communities rather than putting one here, another two or three miles away, and yet another some distance from the others? It seems to me that there is land available, at least in some parts of this country, where community settlement could be put into effect, and I believe that it has much to recommend it. When you settle
one man here and another some miles away, you restrict their opportunities of social life; you lessen the opportunities of providing a suitable education for their children, and you place them under other and great disadvantages. By bringing a group of them into a community you are able to obtain for them better schools, superior educational facilities, improve their opportunities for cooperation and give them better instruction from the government employees who have to serve all those farmers. It seems to me a matter which should be very carefully studied.

All kinds of suggestions were made to the committee of eighteen who discussed these proposals for eighteen months, and these and other proposals for community settlement will be placed before the special committee of this house which is to review the details of this bill, and will receive their careful consideration, although I must say that in my own province, it seems to me, after the last war, group settlements were not very successful.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT

speechtext:
Is this part of a comprehensive plan which seeks to reestablish all the men who are now in the services and, if so, why has agriculture been selected as an industry which should have 180,000,000 expended? At the end of the last war, farm prices were at a very high level; wheat had been selling at $2.50 a bushel, and it was apparent that there was going to be a market for farm products at fairly high prices for a long time, so that men anticipated, in going into this industry, that they would be able to pay for their investment and make a living. We now find ourselves in a period when agriculture is a depressed industry. Farm prices are at very low levels. A person must have a lot of confidence to anticipate that in the next few years there will be markets for unlimited quantities of agricultural products. Has the government considered what will be the effect of spending $80,000,000 in a depressed industry, upon the people who have been struggling for the last ten or even twenty years to meet their interest payments and taxes and remain on the land? It would seem to me that there are other industries in Can-

ada where these sums of money might be spent to better advantage. At the present moment we are experiencing a very serious shortage of steel. We are having difficulty in getting oil. I wonder why agriculture has been selected as the one industry to have such a large expenditure, and in which large numbers of men now in the service may look forward to finding employment and to repaying the amounts which they will receive under this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext: Every point which my hon. friend has mentioned in his remarks was very carefully considered by the committee of eighteen. I do not know whether he has seen the names of the committee who have studied this question. When he says that we are spending money on land settlement alone, he is misinformed. A very moderate view of the order in council of October 1 is that there will be an obligation to this country of at least $100,000,000; the returned soldier will be trained for various types of industry; provision will be made for putting him back to insured employment, on a parity with the man who has stayed at home, in civilian industry, and there are various other benefits. After-war land settlement has required special legislation. This, I think, has been very very carefully considered and reviewed, and it is the hope that it will be not only of great benefit to those who can avail themselves of the opportunities provided under it, but to the national economy as a whole. I do not think the mere fact that prices are depressed at the moment will involve injury to the agricultural industry in the slightest degree. It may be a very good time to lay plans for the future and take advantage of the depressed prices which may prevail at the moment, for the future benefit of the soldier settler-of course, in conjunction with the civilian who is now on the land. There is no intention of injuring the person now on the land; rather, the object is to cooperate with the person now on the land for the benefit of the returned soldier.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's exposition of his plan. I believe he has done a very good job and that his ideas are commendable. I have just been wondering whether he has gone so far as to estimate the number of farmers that Canada really needs. I read the other day a statement concerning the United States to the effect that they had
30.000.	000 farmers and they needed only
24.000.	000. I am wondering whether there is any possibility of our getting more farmers than we really need. My interest in this

question arises probably from the fact that I come from an agricultural constituency, and I have had reason to suspect that there were certain people in the government who were interested in destroying the farmers on the land, in displacing them by any means, torturing them to death if needs be. Perhaps these sound like bitter words, but no one who has been on the soil for forty years can come to any other conclusion when he sees the price structure which obtains at the present time through wide areas of agricultural lands. I am wondering whether the minister has really gone into that matter.
I think a good deal of care should be given to the question whether or not we shall be able to sell as much agricultural produce after the war as we are now selling. If we are not going to be able to sell more wool, for example, more beef, eggs and other agricultural products than we are now selling, and if we are now not producing anywhere nearly as much of these commodities as our present agricultural productive establishment can produce, then it seems to me that we are running a serious risk in very greatly increasing the number of our agricultural producers.
Let me hasten to say that I think there is no finer place in the world for men to be than on the land. There is no finer place to raise a family. There is no happier place to live in, provided conditions are such that one has a chance to make a living. But the minister will be one of the first to agree that those conditions do not obtain in Canada in the agricultural areas.
Unless we can see adequate reason for believing that after the war there will be a sufficiently greatly increased demand for our products to enable us to sell the output of many more farmers than we now have producing, I see no reason for optimism.
Then the question has been brought up once or twice-I merely refer to it here-of price. It would comfort me considerably if the minister or some of his colleagues would indicate to the committee, even by a word, that they see how in this country prices can be established and maintained so that the farmer can be guaranteed, over a period of five years, say, cost of production plus such profit as will enable him to live. The minister has not given any such indication. He may know, but he has certainly kept the secret very well.
Up to the present time our agricultural prices have depended in large measure on prices in world markets such as Liverpool and Chicago. The government are only recently beginning to realize that it must be made possible within the country to govern agricultural prices in the country indepen-

Compulsory Military Service
dently of world market conditions. The moment they begin to govern prices within the country, using only the devices which they now possess, they will place upon the economy of Canada burdens such as the economy will not long sustain. This is the reason for the question I propounded to the minister. I would be, with him, happy in contemplating a greatly increased number of farmers on the land, which I think his scheme will bring into being, if only we could settle the matter of prices. But I contended last year in vain for a price to be fixed on eggs until a certain date in 1942. We were unable then to do that, and the Minister of Agriculture rather scornfully cast a certain amount of aspersion on me because I was so foolish as to insist upon it. The principle is a very simple one. If we cannot establish prices which are fair and remunerative in connection with the various agricultural products, then the minister's whole land settlement scheme will simply blow up like a bubble, because the ability of any farmer whatsoever, soldier or civilian, to subsist on the farm will depend in large measure on his price.
If the minister can give us some idea as to whether or not we have more farmers in Canada than we need, whether he knows how we can maintain prices, whether he has any idea as to how we shall market the goods we produce so that in case we increase by one-third our egg production, butter production, beef or hog production or flax or sugar production

if he can give us some information in these matters, I shall be greatly comforted. If he cannot do so, probably we shall need to look upon his proposal with some restraint.
